match.reason: The closest bank point, Intertextual connections and interpretation, mainly teaches how a link to an older text shapes a reader's reading of one new text, and it also covers structure and devices, which goes beyond the brief. The brief asks students to read texts against each other so that both, and the culture they come from, are understood better, and that idea is not taught in any bank point.

draft.title: Connections between texts
card: Reading texts against each other is called making connections between texts. The link can be a shared theme, a shared form or a reference.
two texts explore the same idea, such as loneliness, in different ways. A poem and a film about a lonely teenager might both say something about belonging.
two texts use the same type of text or structure, such as a diary entry or a sonnet. Comparing how each uses the form shows what each writer chose to do with it.

one text points to another, such as a song that names a famous play. A reader who knows the other text can see extra meaning. Comparing linked texts can deepen understanding of both and of the culture each came from.
draft.remember: Linking texts by theme, form or reference can show new meaning in both.

a.q: A novel and a documentary both explore what it means to feel like an outsider at a new school. What connection do they share?
a.why: Both texts explore the same idea, being an outsider, so the link is a theme. A novel and a documentary are different forms, and neither is said to point to the other.
a.clue: Look at the idea both texts explore, not how they are made.

b.q: Mia reads a poem about a bushfire, then a short story that names the poem in its title. She finds the story gains meaning because she knows the poem. What connection has she used?
b.why: The story points to the poem, so the link is a reference, and knowing the poem adds meaning. Both texts may be about fire, but the meaning Mia gained came from the story naming the poem.
b.clue: One text points directly to the other.
